claim: GtACR2 activation inhibited the soma of mouse cortical neurons.
source: We found that GtACR2 activation inhibited the soma, but unexpectedly depolarized the presynaptic terminals resulting in neurotransmitter release.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that blue light activation of GtACR2 suppressed action potentials evoked by current injections in GtACR2+ neurons (Figure 1C).

claim: GtACR2 activation depolarized the presynaptic terminals resulting in neurotransmitter release.
source: We found that GtACR2 activation inhibited the soma, but unexpectedly depolarized the presynaptic terminals resulting in neurotransmitter release.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing EPSCs in GtACR2- neurons upon GtACR2 activation (Figure 1F,G) and direct evidence of presynaptic terminal depolarization (Figure 3).

claim: Reducing chloride concentrations in the axon and presynaptic terminals diminished GtACR2-induced neurotransmitter release.
source: Reducing the chloride concentrations in the axon and presynaptic terminals diminished the GtACR2-induced neurotransmitter release, indicating an excitatory effect of chloride channels in these compartments.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that bumetanide (NKCC1 inhibitor) diminished GtACR2-induced EPSCs and IPSCs (Figure 2A,B,E,F).

claim: A hybrid somatodendritic targeting motif (Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC) reduced GtACR2-induced neurotransmitter release.
source: A novel hybrid somatodendritic targeting motif reduced the GtACR2-induced neurotransmitter release while enhancing the somatic photocurrents.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced EPSCs in GtACR2- neurons when GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC was used compared to wild type GtACR2 (Figure 5D-G).

claim: The hybrid somatodendritic targeting motif (Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC) enhanced somatic photocurrents.
source: A novel hybrid somatodendritic targeting motif reduced the GtACR2-induced neurotransmitter release while enhancing the somatic photocurrents.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC photocurrents were 2.7-3.5 fold larger than wild type GtACR2 photocurrents (Figure 5A-C).

claim: GtACR2 was present in the soma, dendrites, and axon of layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: We obtained acute coronal brain slices from 3 to 8 week-old mice and observed that GtACR2 was present in the soma, dendrites, and axon (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent imaging data showing GtACR2-EYFP distribution in different neuronal compartments (Figure 1A).

claim: Activation of GtACR2 by wide-field blue light potently inhibited current-induced spiking in GtACR2+ neurons.
source: As previously reported (Govorunova et al., 2015), activation of GtACR2 by wide-field blue light (455 nm) potently inhibited current-induced spiking in these neurons (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 1C) and citation to previous work (Govorunova et al., 2015).

claim: Activation of GtACR2 with a short light pulse generated inward currents in all recorded GtACR2- neurons.
source: Activation of GtACR2 with a short light pulse (0.5–10 ms) generated inward currents in all recorded GtACR2– neurons that were voltage clamped at the reversal potential for GABAergic inhibition (−60 mV).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing EPSCs in GtACR2- neurons (Figure 1F,G).

claim: The onsets of inward currents in GtACR2- neurons followed the onset of blue light by 3.19 ± 0.26 ms.
source: The onsets of these inward currents followed the onset of the blue light by 3.19 ± 0.26 ms (mean ± s.e.m., n = 25).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of EPSC onset latencies.

claim: The inward currents in GtACR2- neurons were abolished by glutamatergic receptor antagonists NBQX and CPP.
source: These currents were abolished by the glutamatergic receptor antagonists, NBQX and CPP (Figure 1F), or the voltage-gated sodium channel blocker, tetrodotoxin (TTX; Figure 1G), indicating that they were indeed monosynaptic EPSCs caused by the glutamate transmitter released from GtACR2+ neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing abolishment of EPSCs by NBQX and CPP (Figure 1F).

claim: The inward currents in GtACR2- neurons were abolished by TTX.
source: These currents were abolished by the glutamatergic receptor antagonists, NBQX and CPP (Figure 1F), or the voltage-gated sodium channel blocker, tetrodotoxin (TTX; Figure 1G), indicating that they were indeed monosynaptic EPSCs caused by the glutamate transmitter released from GtACR2+ neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing abolishment of EPSCs by TTX (Figure 1G).

claim: The inward currents were monosynaptic EPSCs caused by glutamate released from GtACR2+ neurons.
source: These currents were abolished by the glutamatergic receptor antagonists, NBQX and CPP (Figure 1F), or the voltage-gated sodium channel blocker, tetrodotoxin (TTX; Figure 1G), indicating that they were indeed monosynaptic EPSCs caused by the glutamate transmitter released from GtACR2+ neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing short latency, sensitivity to glutamate receptor antagonists, and TTX sensitivity.

claim: Activation of GtACR2 in pyramidal neurons produced disynaptic IPSCs in GtACR2- neurons.
source: Activation of GtACR2 also produced inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in GtACR2– neurons that were voltage clamped at the reversal potential for glutamatergic excitation (+10 mV). These IPSCs were disynaptic because they were abolished by NBQX and CPP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that activating GtACR2 in pyramidal neurons can release sufficient glutamate to recruit inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing IPSCs that were abolished by glutamate receptor antagonists (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Activating GtACR2 in pyramidal neurons can release sufficient glutamate to recruit inhibitory interneurons.
source: These IPSCs were disynaptic because they were abolished by NBQX and CPP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that activating GtACR2 in pyramidal neurons can release sufficient glutamate to recruit inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IPSCs were abolished by glutamate receptor antagonists, indicating they were mediated by glutamate-driven activation of interneurons.

claim: Activation of GtACR2 in Pv neurons generated IPSCs in all recorded GtACR2- layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Using acute brain slices from 3 to 6 week-old mice, we found that activation of GtACR2 in Pv neurons generated IPSCs in all recorded GtACR2– layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, and the IPSCs were abolished by Gabazine, a GABAA receptor antagonist, or TTX (Figure 1I–K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing IPSCs in GtACR2- neurons (Figure 1I-K).

claim: The IPSCs from GtACR2 activation in Pv neurons were abolished by Gabazine.
source: Using acute brain slices from 3 to 6 week-old mice, we found that activation of GtACR2 in Pv neurons generated IPSCs in all recorded GtACR2– layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, and the IPSCs were abolished by Gabazine, a GABAA receptor antagonist, or TTX (Figure 1I–K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 1J).

claim: The IPSCs from GtACR2 activation in Pv neurons were abolished by TTX.
source: Using acute brain slices from 3 to 6 week-old mice, we found that activation of GtACR2 in Pv neurons generated IPSCs in all recorded GtACR2– layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, and the IPSCs were abolished by Gabazine, a GABAA receptor antagonist, or TTX (Figure 1I–K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 1K).

claim: The onsets of IPSCs from GtACR2 activation in Pv neurons followed the onset of blue light by 2.47 ± 0.15 ms.
source: The onsets of the IPSCs followed the onset of the blue light by 2.47 ± 0.15 ms (mean ± s.e.m., n = 17), indicating that they were monosynaptic IPSCs caused by the GABA transmitter released from GtACR2+ Pv neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of IPSC onset latencies.

claim: The IPSCs from GtACR2 activation in Pv neurons were monosynaptic IPSCs caused by GABA released from GtACR2+ Pv neurons.
source: The onsets of the IPSCs followed the onset of the blue light by 2.47 ± 0.15 ms (mean ± s.e.m., n = 17), indicating that they were monosynaptic IPSCs caused by the GABA transmitter released from GtACR2+ Pv neurons.
evidence: Inferred from short latency, sensitivity to GABAA receptor antagonist, and TTX sensitivity.

claim: Repetitive activation of GtACR2 with a high-frequency train of light pulses produced reliable EPSCs or IPSCs.
source: We activated GtACR2 in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons or Pv neurons with a high-frequency train of light pulses and found that each light pulse produced reliable EPSCs or IPSCs, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Continuous activation of GtACR2 with a long pulse of light transiently generated large EPSCs or IPSCs followed by smaller synaptic responses.
source: Interestingly, continuous activation of GtACR2 in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons or Pv neurons with a long pulse of light (e.g., 2 s) transiently generated large EPSCs or IPSCs, respectively, followed by various amounts of smaller synaptic responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B,E,F,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B,E,F,G).

claim: More than 50% of neurotransmitter release occurred within the first 100-200 ms of a 2-s light pulse.
source: Typically, more than 50% of the neurotransmitter release occurred within the first 100–200 ms of the light pulse (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D,H,I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing cumulative charge transfer curves (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D,H,I).

claim: The Nernst equilibrium potential of chloride becomes lower than the action potential threshold in rodent cortical neurons after the second postnatal week.
source: The finding of GtACR2-induced neurotransmitter release was unexpected, because the Nernst equilibrium potential of chloride becomes lower than the action potential threshold in rodent cortical neurons after the second postnatal week, and activation of chloride channels should inhibit, not promote, neurotransmitter release onto neighboring cells (Ben-Ari, 2002; Owens et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Ben-Ari, 2002; Owens et al., 1996).

claim: GtACR2 does not conduct physiological cations in cortical neurons.
source: First, it was reported that GtACR2 did not conduct physiological cations (Govorunova et al., 2015), but some other light-gated chloride channels retained certain cation conductance (Berndt et al., 2014; Wietek et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Govorunova et al., 2015) and verified by experimental data showing similar reversal potentials for GtACR2 and GABAA receptors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: The reversal potentials of GtACR2-mediated photocurrents and GABAergic IPSCs were similar for each neuron and well below the action potential threshold.
source: We found that the reversal potentials of GtACR2-mediated photocurrents and GABAergic IPSCs were similar for each neuron and well below the action potential threshold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), indicating that GtACR2 does not conduct cations to cause neurotransmitter release.
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claim: GtACR2-induced neurotransmitter release is not caused by rebound depolarization.
source: Second, we tested if GtACR2-induced neurotransmitter release could be due to rebound depolarization. An increase in the intracellular chloride caused by GtACR2 activation may trigger rapid efflux of chloride after the blue light illumination terminates. However, this possibility is unlikely because when GtACR2 was activated by a long pulse of blue light, neurotransmitter release occurred before the light illumination ended (see examples in Figure 1F,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing neurotransmitter release during light stimulation (Figure 1F,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Ih currents slightly increased the amplitudes of GtACR2-induced EPSCs.
source: However, pharmacological inhibition of Ih currents slightly increased the amplitudes of GtACR2-induced EPSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B), most likely because inhibiting Ih currents increases neuronal membrane resistances (Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B) and citation to previous work (Robinson and Siegelbaum, 2003).

claim: GtACR2-induced neurotransmitter release requires high concentrations of intracellular chloride.
source: When we activated GtACR2 in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, the resulting EPSCs in GtACR2– pyramidal neurons were diminished by bath application of bumetanide (Figure 2A,B), indicating that GtACR2-induced neurotransmitter release requires high concentrations of intracellular chloride.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that bumetanide (NKCC1 inhibitor) diminished EPSCs (Figure 2A,B).

claim: Bumetanide does not block GtACR2 itself.
source: An alternative interpretation of this result would be that bumetanide blocks GtACR2 itself. To test this possibility, we simultaneously recorded the photocurrents and EPSCs in GtACR2+ and GtACR2– pyramidal neurons, respectively. While bumetanide diminished the EPSCs in GtACR2– neurons, it had no effect on the photocurrents in GtACR2+ neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B), thereby ruling out the possibility that bumetanide affects GtACR2 itself.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no effect of bumetanide on GtACR2 photocurrents (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).

claim: Bumetanide did not affect ChR2-induced EPSCs.
source: Furthermore, when a cation channel, channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) (Boyden et al., 2005; Li et al., 2005; Nagel et al., 2003), was expressed and activated in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, the resulting EPSCs in ChR2– neurons were not affected by bumetanide (Figure 2C,D), indicating that reducing the intracellular chloride concentration only affects chloride-mediated, and not cation-mediated, EPSCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 2C,D).

claim: Bumetanide diminished IPSCs resulting from GtACR2 activation in Pv neurons.
source: Finally, bumetanide also diminished the IPSCs resulting from GtACR2 activation in Pv neurons (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 2E,F).

claim: Light activation of GtACR2 generates an excitatory chloride conductance in certain neuronal compartments to trigger neurotransmitter release.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that light activation of GtACR2 generates an excitatory chloride conductance in certain neuronal compartments to trigger neurotransmitter release.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing bumetanide-sensitive neurotransmitter release.

claim: Acute expression of GtACR2 in mature neurons produced bumetanide-sensitive EPSCs.
source: We obtained acute coronal brain slices 1–3 weeks after injecting Flpo-expressing AAV and found that light activation of GtACR2, again, produced bumetanide-sensitive EPSCs in GtACR2– neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E). Thus, it is unlikely that GtACR2 expression during neuronal development alters the chloride homeostasis to render GtACR2 excitatory, as acute expression of GtACR2 in mature neurons had the same effect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).

claim: Light activation of iC++ generated EPSCs in iC++- layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons that were abolished by NBQX and CPP.
source: Similar to GtACR2, light activation of iC++ generated EPSCs in iC++– layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons that were abolished by NBQX and CPP (amplitude reduced by 97.3 ± 0.9%, mean ± s.e.m., n = 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing EPSCs abolished by glutamate receptor antagonists.

claim: Bumetanide diminished iC++-induced EPSCs.
source: Bumetanide diminished the iC++-induced EPSCs (Figure 2G,H) without affecting the iC++-mediated photocurrents (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 2G,H).

claim: Light activation of iC++ in Pv neurons caused bumetanide-sensitive IPSCs in iC++- layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: We also expressed iC++ in Pv neurons by injecting a Cre-dependent AAV into PvalbCre/+ mice and found that light activation of iC++ caused bumetanide-sensitive IPSCs in iC++– layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 2I,J).

claim: Activation of iChloC in Pv neurons resulted in IPSCs in 10 out of 17 recorded iChloC- layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Similarly, when we expressed iChloC in Pv neurons, light activation of iChloC resulted in IPSCs in 10 out of 17 recorded iChloC– layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons (183 ± 42 pA, mean ± s.e.m., n = 10), presumably because iChloC generated smaller photocurrents than iC++ (iChloC, 292 ± 62 pA, n = 7; iC++, 2182 ± 291 pA, n = 15; recorded at the membrane potential of +10 mV; mean ± s.e.m., p<0.0001, t test with Welch's correction).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing IPSCs in a subset of neurons and comparison of photocurrent amplitudes.

claim: Activation of GtACR1 in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons produced EPSCs onto all recorded GtACR1- pyramidal neurons.
source: Finally, activation of GtACR1 in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons produced EPSCs onto all recorded GtACR1– pyramidal neurons (149 ± 47 pA, mean ± s.e.m., n = 11).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing EPSCs in all recorded neurons.

claim: Activation of different light-gated chloride channels in neurons can trigger neurotransmitter release.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that activation of different light-gated chloride channels in neurons can trigger neurotransmitter release.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing neurotransmitter release for GtACR2, GtACR1, iC++, and iChloC.

claim: Activation of presynaptic GABAA or glycine receptors enhanced neurotransmitter release at several synapses of the hippocampus, cerebellum, and brainstem.
source: First, activation of presynaptic GABAA or glycine receptors enhanced neurotransmitter release at several synapses of the hippocampus, cerebellum, and brainstem (Jang et al., 2006; Pugh and Jahr, 2011; Ruiz et al., 2010; Stell et al., 2007; Turecek and Trussell, 2001; Zorrilla de San Martin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Jang et al., 2006; Pugh and Jahr, 2011; Ruiz et al., 2010; Stell et al., 2007; Turecek and Trussell, 2001; Zorrilla de San Martin et al., 2017).

claim: Chloride concentrations were 4-5 times higher in the presynaptic terminals of the Calyx of Held than the parent soma.
source: Second, the chloride concentrations were 4–5 times higher in the presynaptic terminals of the Calyx of Held than the parent soma (Price and Trussell, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Price and Trussell, 2006).

claim: There is an axo-somato-dendritic gradient in which the reversal potentials of GABA from the axon to the soma and dendrites of cortical neurons become progressively more negative.
source: Third, there appeared to be an axo-somato-dendritic gradient in which the reversal potentials of GABA from the axon to the soma and dendrites of cortical neurons become progressively more negative (Khirug et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Khirug et al., 2008).

claim: Light activation of GtACR2 in the callosal projections generated EPSCs in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons of the contralateral cortex.
source: Light activation of GtACR2 in the callosal projections generated EPSCs in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons of the contralateral cortex, which were diminished by TTX (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C) or bumetanide (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).

claim: Activation of GtACR2 in the axon and presynaptic terminals is sufficient to trigger neurotransmitter release.
source: These results demonstrate that activation of GtACR2 in the axon and presynaptic terminals is sufficient to trigger neurotransmitter release.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing EPSCs from activation of severed callosal axons (Figure 3B).

claim: In the absence of action potentials, light activation of GtACR2 is sufficient to depolarize the presynaptic membrane to open voltage-gated calcium channels and trigger neurotransmitter release.
source: However, when we further blocked voltage-gated potassium channels by 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) and tetraethylammonium (TEA) to prolong membrane depolarization (Petreanu et al., 2009), the EPSCs and IPSCs were partially recovered (Figure 3D,F). These results indicate that in the absence of action potentials, light activation of GtACR2 is sufficient to depolarize the presynaptic membrane to open voltage-gated calcium channels and trigger neurotransmitter release.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing partial recovery of EPSCs and IPSCs with 4-AP and TEA in the presence of TTX (Figure 3D,F).

claim: GtACR2-induced axonal depolarization can evoke antidromic action potentials.
source: We further tested if GtACR2-induced axonal depolarization could evoke antidromic action potentials by performing extracellular loose-patch or whole-cell current clamp recordings at the somas of GtACR2+ pyramidal neurons. We observed antidromic spikes in 9 out of 88 neurons recorded in loose-patch configuration and 21 out of 56 neurons recorded in whole-cell configuration in response to blue light stimulation (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing antidromic spikes in a subset of GtACR2+ neurons (Figure 3G,H).

claim: The antidromic spikes were generated within the GtACR2+ neurons, rather than by excitatory inputs from other neurons.
source: The antidromic spikes were not affected by NBQX and CPP, but were abolished by TTX (Figure 3H), indicating that the spikes were generated within the GtACR2+ neurons, rather than by excitatory inputs from other neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that antidromic spikes were insensitive to glutamate receptor antagonists but abolished by TTX (Figure 3H).

claim: TlcnC and Kv2.1C were most effective in targeting GtACR2 to the soma and dendrites among tested motifs.
source: Among tested motifs, TlcnC and Kv2.1C were most effective in targeting GtACR2 to the soma and dendrites (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced EYFP fluorescence ratio between layer 5 and layer 2/3 (Figure 4D).

claim: Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC was the best in restricting GtACR2 within the somatodendritic domain.
source: As these two motifs may engage different trafficking mechanisms, we combined them to create two hybrid motifs, Kv2.1C-TlcnC and Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC. Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC turned out to be the best in restricting GtACR2 within the somatodendritic domain (Figure 4A,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing the lowest normalized EYFP fluorescence ratio for Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC (Figure 4A,D).

claim: GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C and GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC showed less intracellular aggregation than wild type GtACR2.
source: Interestingly, GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C and GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC showed less intracellular aggregation than wild type GtACR2 (Figure 4B), suggesting that the somatodendritic targeting motifs also enhance the surface expression of GtACR2.
evidence: Supported by fluorescent imaging data (Figure 4B).

claim: The EYFP fluorescence of the callosal projections in the contralateral hemisphere was reduced for GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C and GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC compared to GtACR2-EYFP.
source: Finally, the EYFP fluorescence of the callosal projections in the contralateral hemisphere was also reduced for GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C and GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC as compared to GtACR2-EYFP (Figure 4C,E), demonstrating that both somatodendritic targeting motifs decreased the trafficking of GtACR2 into the distal axon.
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 4C,E).

claim: The blue light-activated photocurrents of GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C were 2.1-2.4 fold larger than GtACR2-EYFP photocurrents.
source: We first recorded GtACR2+ layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons and found that the blue light-activated photocurrents of GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C and GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC were 2.1–2.4 and 2.7–3.5 folds of GtACR2-EYFP photocurrents, respectively (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,C,E,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 5A-C).

claim: The blue light-activated photocurrents of GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC were 2.7-3.5 fold larger than GtACR2-EYFP photocurrents.
source: We first recorded GtACR2+ layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons and found that the blue light-activated photocurrents of GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C and GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC were 2.1–2.4 and 2.7–3.5 folds of GtACR2-EYFP photocurrents, respectively (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,C,E,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 5A-C).

claim: The EPSCs evoked by activating GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C were reduced by 52-60% compared to those evoked by activating GtACR2-EYFP.
source: We then recorded the EPSCs in GtACR2– layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in response to different strengths of blue light stimulation. The EPSCs evoked by activating GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C or GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC were reduced by 52–60% or 65–77%, respectively, as compared to those evoked by activating GtACR2-EYFP (Figure 5D–G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D,F,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 5D-G).

claim: The EPSCs evoked by activating GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC were reduced by 65-77% compared to those evoked by activating GtACR2-EYFP.
source: We then recorded the EPSCs in GtACR2– layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in response to different strengths of blue light stimulation. The EPSCs evoked by activating GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C or GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC were reduced by 52–60% or 65–77%, respectively, as compared to those evoked by activating GtACR2-EYFP (Figure 5D–G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D,F,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 5D-G).

claim: When photostimulating the callosal projections, the EPSCs were reduced by 54% and 73% for GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C and GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC, respectively, compared to GtACR2-EYFP.
source: Furthermore, when photostimulating the callosal projections, the EPSCs in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons of the contralateral cortex were reduced by 54% and 73% for GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C and GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC, respectively, as compared to GtACR2-EYFP (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 5H,I).

claim: The somatodendritic targeting motifs shift GtACR2 from the axon towards the soma and dendrites, thereby reducing the excitatory action in the axon and presynaptic terminals while enhancing the inhibitory currents at the soma and dendrites.
source: These results show that the somatodendritic targeting motifs, especially Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC, shift GtACR2 from the axon towards the soma and dendrites, thereby reducing the excitatory action in the axon and presynaptic terminals while enhancing the inhibitory currents at the soma and dendrites.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing reduced EPSCs and increased photocurrents for somatodendritically targeted GtACR2 variants.

claim: Wide-field activation of light-gated chloride channels in cortical neurons suppresses action potentials at the soma but also triggers neurotransmitter release at the presynaptic terminals.
source: Our experiments reveal that wide-field activation of these channels in cortical neurons suppresses action potentials at the soma but also triggers neurotransmitter release at the presynaptic terminals, thereby voiding inhibition of neuronal activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing both somatic inhibition and presynaptic neurotransmitter release.

claim: The excitatory action of chloride channels in the axon and presynaptic terminals is due to high intracellular chloride concentrations that create a depolarizing chloride electrochemical gradient.
source: As demonstrated, the excitatory action of chloride channels in the axon and presynaptic terminals is due to the high intracellular chloride concentrations that create a depolarizing chloride electrochemical gradient.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing bumetanide-sensitive neurotransmitter release and direct depolarization of presynaptic terminals.

claim: The depolarizing effect of presynaptic chloride channels has been documented at a few synapses in the hippocampus, cerebellum, and brainstem through application of agonists or antagonists.
source: The depolarizing effect of presynaptic chloride channels, GABAA or glycine receptors, has been documented at a few synapses in the hippocampus, cerebellum, and brainstem through application of agonists or antagonists (Jang et al., 2006; Pugh and Jahr, 2011; Ruiz et al., 2010; Stell et al., 2007; Turecek and Trussell, 2001; Zorrilla de San Martin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Jang et al., 2006; Pugh and Jahr, 2011; Ruiz et al., 2010; Stell et al., 2007; Turecek and Trussell, 2001; Zorrilla de San Martin et al., 2017).

claim: A presynaptic depolarizing chloride electrochemical gradient is likely a general property across brain regions and neuronal types.
source: Our results in cortical excitatory and inhibitory neurons expand previous findings and indicate that a presynaptic depolarizing chloride electrochemical gradient is likely a general property across brain regions and neuronal types.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data in cortical excitatory and inhibitory neurons and previous findings in other brain regions.

claim: Activation of presynaptic chloride channels can elicit action potentials with short latency.
source: More importantly, our experiments directly demonstrate that activation of presynaptic chloride channels is in fact excitatory, as it can elicit action potentials with short latency, which was difficult to explicitly demonstrate by agonist application (Pugh and Jahr, 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing antidromic spikes (Figure 3G-J) and citation to previous work (Pugh and Jahr, 2011).

claim: Light-gated chloride channels can be targeted to different brain regions, cell types, and subcellular compartments to study chloride electrochemical gradients with unprecedented temporal precision.
source: Thus, light-gated chloride channels can be targeted to different brain regions, cell types, and subcellular compartments to study chloride electrochemical gradients with unprecedented temporal precision.
evidence: Inferred from the demonstrated ability to activate chloride channels with light and observe their effects in specific compartments.

claim: GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC is the most improved light-gated chloride channel for optogenetic inhibition.
source: While GtACR2-EYFP-Kv2.1C-linker-TlcnC can still traffic to the axon to cause neurotransmitter release, it is thus far the most improved light-gated chloride channel for optogenetic inhibition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced neurotransmitter release and enhanced somatic photocurrents compared to wild type GtACR2.

claim: It is possible to identify a light stimulation strength that does not cause neurotransmitter release but still produces large inhibitory photocurrents in GtACR2+ neurons.
source: Supporting this idea, post hoc analysis of our experiments indicates that, for a given experiment, it is possible to identify a light stimulation strength that is low enough not to cause neurotransmitter release but still produce large inhibitory photocurrents in GtACR2+ neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: During continuous activation of GtACR2, large and synchronous neurotransmitter release occurs at the early phase of light stimulation.
source: Furthermore, since during continuous activation of GtACR2, large and synchronous neurotransmitter release occurs at the early phase of the light stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), one may also take advantage of the late phase when neurotransmitter release is reduced but photocurrent is still robust for optogenetic inhibition experiments.
evidence: Supported by experimental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

claim: GtACR1 and GtACR2 are increasingly used due to their large photocurrents and high sensitivity to light.
source: Light-gated chloride channels, particularly GtACR1 and GtACR2, are increasingly used due to their large photocurrents and high sensitivity to light (Forli et al., 2018; Mardinly et al., 2018; Mauss et al., 2017; Mohamed et al., 2017; Mohammad et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent work (Forli et al., 2018; Mardinly et al., 2018; Mauss et al., 2017; Mohamed et al., 2017; Mohammad et al., 2017).

claim: Light-gated chloride channels allow multiple ions to cross the membrane per photocycle.
source: Light-gated chloride channels, such as Guillardia theta anion channelrhodopsin 1 and 2 (GtACR1 and GtACR2), iC++, and iChloC, overcome these limitations (Berndt et al., 2014; Govorunova et al., 2015, 2017b; Wietek et al., 2014). They are highly sensitive to light, allow multiple ions to cross the membrane per photocycle, and reduce membrane resistance, thereby potently inhibiting action potentials.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Berndt et al., 2014; Govorunova et al., 2015, 2017b; Wietek et al., 2014).

claim: Light-gated chloride channels reduce membrane resistance.
source: They are highly sensitive to light, allow multiple ions to cross the membrane per photocycle, and reduce membrane resistance, thereby potently inhibiting action potentials.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and established knowledge about ion channels.

claim: Light-driven inward chloride pumps and outward proton pumps transport only one ion per absorbed photon.
source: The widely used light-driven inward chloride pumps and outward proton pumps, such as Natronomonas pharaonis halorhodopsin (NpHR) and Halorubrum sodomense archaerhodopsin (Arch), can hyperpolarize membrane potentials, independent of the electrochemical gradients, to inhibit action potentials with millisecond precision (Chow et al., 2010; Chuong et al., 2014; Han and Boyden, 2007; Han et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2007). However, their efficacies are limited because only one ion is transported per absorbed photon, and their activation does not decrease membrane resistance.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Chow et al., 2010; Chuong et al., 2014; Han and Boyden, 2007; Han et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2007).

claim: Activation of eNpHR3.0 can transiently change the reversal potential of GABAA receptors and alter inhibitory synaptic inputs.
source: For example, activation of a light-driven inward chloride pump, eNpHR3.0, can transiently change the reversal potential of GABAA receptors and alter the inhibitory synaptic inputs (Raimondo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Raimondo et al., 2012).

claim: Prolonged activation of eArch3.0 can increase presynaptic calcium concentrations and spontaneous neurotransmitter release.
source: Prolonged activation of a light-driven outward proton pump, eArch3.0, can increase presynaptic calcium concentrations and spontaneous neurotransmitter release (Mahn et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Mahn et al., 2016).

claim: The effect of light-gated chloride channels depends on the difference between the membrane potential and the reversal potential for chloride.
source: Therefore, it is also crucial to thoroughly characterize light-gated chloride channels, as their effect depends on the difference between the membrane potential and the reversal potential for chloride, both of which can vary in different neuronal types and subcellular compartments (Marty and Llano, 2005; Trigo et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Marty and Llano, 2005; Trigo et al., 2008) and established knowledge about ion channels.

claim: Photostimulation of neurons expressing GtACR1 or GtACR2 can paradoxically release neurotransmitters or generate action potentials.
source: These data explain the recent observations that photostimulation of neurons expressing GtACR1 or GtACR2 can paradoxically release neurotransmitters or generate action potentials (Mahn et al., 2016; Malyshev et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Mahn et al., 2016; Malyshev et al., 2017).

claim: Restricting the localization of light-gated chloride channels to the somatodendritic domain improves the inhibitory efficacy of these optogenetic tools.
source: Thus, restricting the localization of light-gated chloride channels to the somatodendritic domain improves the inhibitory efficacy of these optogenetic tools.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing reduced neurotransmitter release and enhanced somatic photocurrents for somatodendritically targeted GtACR2.
